title: The common answer: foreknowledge imposes no necessity, for things are not future because foreknown
source_text: XXIII. Ad hoc Respondent plurimi Christianarum Scholarum Theologi, & recte quidem meo judicio, praescientiam Dei nullam imponere rebus necessitatem: nec enim illam esse rerum causam, sed potius res ipsas futuras illius causam certa ratione dici posse: Videlicet, quia res non ideo futurae sunt, quoniam Deus illas futuras esse praescit; Sed contra Deus illas futuras esse praescit, quia revera futurae sunt.
pass_a_gloss: XXIII. To this very many Theologians of the Christian Schools respond, and rightly indeed in my judgement, that the foreknowledge of God imposes no necessity on things: for that it is not the cause of things, but rather that the future things themselves can in a certain manner be said to be its cause: That is, because things are not therefore future, because God foreknows them to be future; But on the contrary God foreknows them to be future, because they are truly future.
pass_b_english: Very many theologians of the Christian schools answer this, and in my judgement rightly, that God's foreknowledge places no necessity on things. Foreknowledge is not the cause of things; rather, in a certain sense the future things themselves can be called its cause.
Things are not future because God foreknows that they will be. On the contrary, God foreknows that they will be because they really are future.

lemmas.latin: praescientiam Dei nullam imponere rebus necessitatem
lemmas.gloss: the foreknowledge of God imposes no necessity on things

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.
